create-evaluation-set.title: Turn user promises into test cases

sections.title: A demo is one success; an evaluation tests a promise
sections.content:
Your assistant worked once. Now test whether it consistently respects the budget, preserves corrections, excludes unavailable dishes, and waits for approval. Each promise needs a case that could expose a failure.

A golden dataset is a curated collection of inputs and expected outcomes. It need not start large. Include ordinary requests, edge cases, and failures. Keep the expected outcome separate from what the current implementation happens to do.

sections.alt: A checklist and trace reveal which assistant behavior needs improvement.
sections.caption: Test the outcome, trace the failure, and improve one thing.

sections.question: Which is the strongest budget test?

options.text: Every returned sample total is strictly below the stated cap.
The assistant says the word budget.

sections.explanation: The test directly checks the promised constraint.

sections.title: Specify outcomes rather than one exact sentence
sections.content:
For a no-result case, acceptable behavior is an empty shortlist with an explanation. It need not use one fixed sentence. For totals, exact arithmetic is appropriate. Choose the comparison based on the behavior.

The Evaluation Lab runs executable checks on the same core used by retrieval and workflow. It reports each case and an aggregate pass count. These are deterministic component checks, not evidence that an unconnected language model is reliable.

sections.question: Match each case to the promise it tests.

pairs.left: Unavailable item with a high relevance score

sections.explanation: Choose a case capable of breaking the specific promise.

sections.title: Write cases before editing the solution
sections.content:
Create a $25 strict-boundary case, a vegetarian filter case, and an unapproved-submission case. Predict each result before running the lab. If the implementation fails, preserve the test while investigating the cause.

Anthropic’s evaluation guide emphasizes evaluating agent behavior beyond a single plausible final answer. Our small project follows that principle with explicit outcomes and traces.

sections.question: Write an expected result for a search where nothing qualifies.
sections.sample_answer: Return no eligible items, explain the relevant exclusions, and ask before changing a constraint. Do not invent a matching result.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

choose-evaluation-graders.title: Use code, rubrics, and model judges appropriately

sections.title: Different claims need different graders
sections.content:
Use code to check totals, allowed transitions, and whether an unavailable item slipped through. Use a rubric for a subjective property such as whether an explanation makes the tradeoff understandable.

A grader is the mechanism that assesses a result. Human review can establish example judgments. A model judge can help assess open-ended outputs, but its decisions also need checking. Do not replace exact arithmetic with another model’s opinion.

sections.question: Which grader should verify the sum of integer price components?
sections.explanation: Exact numeric requirements should use exact checks.

sections.title: A rubric needs observable anchors
sections.content:
For explanation quality, define 0: unsupported or misleading; 1: accurate but misses the main tradeoff; 2: accurate, sourced, and explains the relevant tradeoff. Supply examples at each level so graders share an interpretation.

If you use a model judge, compare its judgments with human-labeled cases and inspect disagreements. Watch for irrelevant preferences such as rewarding verbosity. Evaluate the judge on the task rather than assuming a model name makes it reliable.

sections.question: Match the criterion to a suitable grading approach.
sections.explanation: Choose the mechanism that can actually observe the criterion.

sections.title: Keep critical failures separate from style scores
sections.content:
An elegant explanation cannot compensate for submitting without approval. Report critical gates separately from average quality. The lab shows a gate failure explicitly instead of hiding it inside a composite score.

In your reflection, grade two fictional recommendations using the rubric. Record the evidence for each score. If your interpretation changes, revise the rubric and regrade the same examples.

sections.question: Why should approval failures stay outside an average style score?
sections.sample_answer: They violate a required permission boundary. A high explanation score must not cancel out an unauthorized action, so approval is a separate release gate.
key_points: Style cannot compensate for unauthorized action

inspect-execution-traces.title: Find the first wrong step in a trace

sections.title: The final answer shows the symptom
sections.content:
A recommendation exceeds the budget. Was the budget extracted incorrectly, did fees go missing, or did a filter fail? A trace records the meaningful execution steps so you can find the first divergence.

For this project, inspect the input constraints, candidate IDs, exclusions, draft version, approval, and submission status. You need observable operations and outcomes, not hidden model reasoning.

sections.question: A final answer is over budget. What is the most useful next step?

options.text: Inspect extraction, price components, and filtering to locate the first error.

sections.explanation: Trace the failure to its originating component before changing unrelated behavior.

sections.title: Log enough to debug without collecting everything
sections.content:
A useful event includes a request or run ID, step name, outcome, duration, and safe metadata. Avoid recording credentials, payment details, or unnecessary personal information. Redaction and retention choices belong in the design.

The Workflow Lab records in-memory events for the fixture run. It does not send telemetry. Use the sequence to explain whether a failure happened before a draft, during approval, or after simulated acceptance.

sections.statement: A useful application trace requires saving every private input and the model’s hidden reasoning.
sections.explanation: Log observable steps and safe metadata needed for diagnosis; minimize sensitive information.

sections.title: Change the earliest faulty component
sections.content:
If the price calculation omitted delivery, changing the recommendation wording will not repair the total. Reproduce the failure, locate the earliest incorrect value, fix that component, and rerun the original case.

A useful bug report contains the request, expected outcome, relevant trace events, actual outcome, and a narrow hypothesis. That is more actionable than “the agent is bad.”

sections.question: Write a concise bug hypothesis for missing delivery fees.
sections.sample_answer: The quote step appears to sum only item prices. I will compare the recorded components with the final total and add a case where delivery pushes the order over budget.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

set-release-gates.title: Decide whether an improvement is ready to ship

sections.title: A better average can hide a worse product
sections.content:
Imagine a change makes most answers faster but occasionally removes a dietary constraint. Report quality by important case categories, not just one average. A change is acceptable only if it satisfies the critical requirements.

Track task success, constraint violations, recovery behavior, latency, and cost separately. For live systems, percentile latency can reveal slow experiences hidden by the mean. The local lab timing is component execution time, not network or model latency.

sections.question: Nine tests pass and the approval gate fails. What should your decision be?

options.text: Block release until the critical permission failure is fixed.
Hide the failing case from the average.

sections.explanation: A critical permission requirement is a gate, not a compensable preference.

sections.title: Compare a baseline with a controlled change
sections.content:
The Evaluation Lab offers baseline, omitted-fee bug, and missing-approval bug variants. The same cases run against each variant. Your job is to explain which promise each failure breaks.

A small fixture suite is a starting point, not proof of universal safety. Define additional representative requests and repeated live-model trials before relying on stochastic behavior. A passing test can only cover what it actually exercised.

sections.statement: Passing a small deterministic fixture suite proves that a live model will handle every future request correctly.
sections.explanation: The suite covers specific deterministic behaviors. Live-model variability and unseen cases require separate evaluation.

sections.title: Write a release decision with a rollback condition
sections.content:
For this prototype, require all critical fixture checks to pass and document remaining live-integration gaps. In a real rollout, start small, monitor the same important behaviors, and define a condition that pauses or rolls back the release.

Your module artifact is an evaluation report: baseline results, one intentionally broken variant, root cause, and a release decision. Export the lab report and save your interpretation in Learnable.

sections.question: State a rollout stop condition for the dinner assistant.
sections.sample_answer: Pause consequential actions if any submission occurs without approval of the current cart version, then inspect the trace and restore the last verified behavior.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.
